title: I Want to Hold Aono-kun so Badly I Could Die
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: High schooler Yuri Kariya loses her new boyfriend Ryuhei Aono to a car accident two weeks into their relationship. When she tries to end her life, Aono returns as a ghost who begs her to live, and they continue a relationship in which they cannot touch. Aono's ghost grows a darker second self that possesses people and pulls at Yuri, while his friend Fujimoto and horror fan Mio investigate.
life_message: Love that refuses to let go can turn destructive; living on and facing grief and family wounds is the harder, truer path.

content.note: Bloody gashes appear on Yuri's body; possession endangers others (ANN review; AniList Body Horror tag).

Suicide attempt and self-harm depicted; not presented as a solution, Aono asks her to live (Wikipedia).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No honor code; conflicts are inner and supernatural, not insults to answer.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Teens act outside adult oversight; families shown as harmful rather than guiding.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Yuri's bond to Aono and damaging family ties outweigh wider community.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Peer friendships; parents' authority shown as abusive (ANN).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Purity ideas across religions mixed with modern school life (ANN).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Emotional truth and personal love prioritized over security.

folkways.japan: Ideas of ritual purity and impurity, and ghosts tied to unfinished attachment, draw on Japanese folk and Shinto-Buddhist ideas about the dead, described here as context.

delivery.evidence: ANN praises the romance-horror blend and finds themes of purity and unhappy families; no preachiness noted in reviews read.
delivery.note: Its views on grief and obsessive love come through the plot rather than speeches.

winners_losers: Sympathy stays with Yuri and the friends trying to save her; clinging love and abusive families are shown as costly.
